correctness.rationale: For the revised claim, the iid individual-absence probabilities give S(a)=(1-q)(1+G_n(q)) for (1,n), with q=1-a. The quotient derivative numerator is n(n-1)q^(n-2)(1+G_n)-(1+nq^(n-1))G_n'. For n>=3 its possible term of degree 2n-3 cancels; at lower degrees the printed coefficients are strictly negative through n-3 then strictly positive through 2n-4. At q=0 it is -1, and at q=1 the numerator is n(n-1)(n+1)/2 because G_n'(1)=n(n-1)/2. Descartes plus the endpoint signs gives one simple positive root in (0,1), and dq/da=-1 gives the strict global minimum in area. The n=1 and n=2 cases are constant and strictly decreasing, respectively. For n=3, solving 3q²+10q-1=0 gives the stated exact area. The census <=3 partitions are exhausted by all singletons, a single species, and (1,2). A single species with n>=2 has positive derivative in q since (n-1)G_n-qG_n' is positive, and all singleton cases are constant. Thus no smaller census can turn, whereas (1,3) does. The retained endpoint corollary is also correct: differentiating aS'/S at a=1 uses S=s, S'=r1, S''=-2r2, and a sign persists by continuity. The supplied script was read, not run; its radical comparison uses floating point, while the exact value follows from the quadratic. The proof independently establishes the universal claims.

value.rationale: The revised finding classifies scale-dependent elasticity for a natural extreme abundance pattern and shows exactly when a reversal is possible at the smallest total population. Even in a model with no spatial interaction, the local exponent can reverse; separating that effect from an assumed fixed log–log slope is useful. The all-n uniqueness and global census boundary, not the routine terminal derivative in isolation, support the value judgment.
